Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette:
Margaret is a 58-year-old woman who lives alone in the small house she once shared with her husband, Frank. Two years ago, Frank was driving them home from a dinner out when a driver ran a red light and smashed into the passenger side of their sedan. Margaret remembers the sound of twisting metal, the shattering glass, and the sudden, crushing pressure against her ribs. She remembers the smell of gasoline and something metallic, possibly blood, though she cannot say whether it was Frank's or her own. She remembers the ambulance arriving, the paramedics prying open the door, the frantic voices. She does not remember much after that, except the hazy waiting room at the hospital and a doctor's face telling her that Frank had died before reaching the emergency department.

In the weeks after the accident, Margaret struggled to sleep. She would lie awake in bed, listening for sounds that were out of place, certain that someone was moving outside. She began checking the locks on all the doors and windows repeatedly before bed, sometimes getting up two or three times in a night to confirm they were secure. Any unexpected movement near her-a sudden gesture from a neighbor, a branch scraping the windowpane-would make her flinch so violently that she felt as though she were back in the car, bracing for impact. She tried not to think about the accident, but the memory would invade without warning. She would be washing dishes or watching television, and suddenly the smell of gasoline would fill her nose, so vivid that she gagged. At other times, she would catch a glimpse of a dented car on the road or hear a siren in the distance, and her heart would pound, her palms would sweat, and she would feel disoriented, as if the event were happening again right then.

The more she tried to avoid these intrusions, the more they seemed to multiply. She stopped driving entirely-every car on the road looked like a potential threat. She stopped taking the bus after a route took her past the intersection where the accident occurred. Ambulances became unbearable: she would cross the street or duck into a store whenever she heard one approaching. Anniversaries were the worst. On the first anniversary of Frank's death, she spent the entire day in her bedroom, curtains drawn, too afraid to step outside. She would later say that she couldn't explain why she was so afraid; she simply knew that if she let herself remember too vividly, she would lose the fragile control she had built.

Her unemployment had started before the accident-she was laid off from her clerical job a few months earlier-but after the trauma, any thought of looking for work felt impossible. She could not face the idea of sitting in an office, unable to concentrate, startled by colleagues walking behind her chair, struggling to keep her composure when a car alarm sounded outside. Over time, she saw less and less of her friends and her two adult children. They called and texted, but she let the messages pile up, afraid that conversation might drift toward Frank, toward the accident, toward anything that would bring the memory flooding back. She had come to believe that she was broken, that she would never feel safe again, and that the only way to protect herself was to stay hidden.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was an anniversary that she could not simply wait out. The two-year mark was approaching, and she found herself unable to sleep, her appetite gone, her body taut with an anticipatory dread she could not name. One afternoon, a neighbor accidentally backed their car into a trash can on the street, and the hollow thud sent Margaret into a full panic attack-she ended up sobbing on her kitchen floor, convinced that she had heard Frank's car being hit again. It was then that she called a crisis line and made an appointment with a clinic. She is terrified that treatment will force her to talk about the accident, to relive what she has worked so hard to push away, but she is equally terrified that if she does not find a way to stop the constant checking, the startles, the smells that come from nowhere, she will lose the last threads of the life she is still trying to hold together.
